告訴那些仍不聽我話的人：在我們古老傳統的律法中，即使對待要屠宰的動物，也規定要給予迅速的死亡，以減輕動物的痛苦。我們的傳統律法對待動物尚且如此，對待戰俘若連動物都不如，便是對神明所立法律的極大冒犯，亦是對神明本身的極大褻瀆。他們的丈夫與兒子死於戰場，已受到神明的注視，這是莫大的榮幸；他們那些多餘的不必要舉動，只會減損家人用生命換來的榮耀，神明必對此感到不悅。若他們再不停止對神明的冒犯，即便我對他們不加處置，神明也會收回他們家族的榮耀，並施予懲罰，因為他們正以神明律法之名行冒犯之事。次子： 我明白了，父親。先知： 那個女祭司怎樣了？次子： 她沒有接受終生監禁的條件，在她的神廟中自焚而死了。先知望著黃昏的落日，戰場上的血腥味似乎能傳到他這裡，即使兩者的實際距離非常遙遠。他那已長大成人的英俊次子沒有說話，他知道父親時常會像這樣陷入靜靜的沉思。昨晚他才剛帶領族人與敵人作戰，至今仍未闔眼，但他強令自己保持警醒，因為父親說過，戰場上的勝利只是另一個開始。他一直很聽父親的話，無比敬重且敬畏著身為先知的父親——在他的記憶中，父親從未出錯。長久的靜默之後，髮絲半黑半白的先知才再次開口說話。先知： 在她還是一個小女孩的時候，我就見過她。次子： 敵人的那個女祭司？先知： 是她。那是在幾個彼此缺乏信任的鬆散聯盟所舉行的會議上，她那時還不到十歲，卻已被內定為下一任的最高大祭司。我們多年的敵人當時已找不到更合適的人選，最後只能依憑稀薄疏遠的血脈，來挑選他們最重要的祭司 (ἱέρεια = priestess)。先知： 起初我還在想，敵人多年來的不義終究引來了眾神的憤怒，他們已然氣數已盡、後繼無人，只要再過一段時間，我們就能徹底擊敗他們。先知的孩子沒有接話，他熟知父親的習慣，知道這個停頓是為了讓他順著父親的回憶去思考。先知： 但當我看到她的第一眼，我就知道我想錯了。這個尚未成年的小女孩將來必定會讓我們的敵人變得更加強大，令他們更難被戰勝。她的早慧根本未曾對我們掩飾，這或許正是她對那些年長她許多的人所發出的第一個警告？先知： 但其實她也沒說過甚麼話。到了最後，令我印象最深的，反而是她問我：「尊敬的先知，我不怕死，但是有點怕痛。您覺得在烈火中死去，痛苦嗎？」突然間，一種異常的恐慌襲向了先知的孩子。這種恐慌對他而言是如此陌生，即使在戰場上與敵人廝殺時也不曾感受過。先知： 穩住，我的好孩子！你是我們族中未來的領袖，你不能動搖，你不可以動搖！即便再恐慌，你也絕不能後退一步！你明白嗎？次子： 是，父親。先知： 在見過她之後，我曾動過派人毒殺她的念頭，但這個念頭很快就打消了。一方面，殺死一位神明的祭司——即便那是虛假的神明——也必須慎之又慎，這是我們的律法傳統；另一方面，她畢竟還只是一個小女孩，暗殺有違我們的傳統習俗與先知律法。而最後真正讓我打消下毒念頭的，是你的兄長。你的兄長……絲毫不遜色於她。她的族人多行不義多年，內部墮落且渙散，而我們的族人正處於興盛之中；只要你同樣早慧的兄長在，她就不會對我們構成威脅。更何況她在族中的地位與威望遠不如我們家族，她根本不可能發揮出全部的力量。聽到父親提及失蹤多年的兄長，次子的情緒再次不由自主地波動起來。兄長多年來都是族中的禁忌，他沒想到父親會在此時再次提起自己敬愛的哥哥。先知： 我的孩子，我知道你多年來一直想明白，為什麼那個曾被我寄予厚望的兄長，最終卻被我親手放逐，並下令永世不得回歸。先知： 這個秘密我未曾向族中任何人透露過。那些祭司家族、諸多長老、出色的戰士，乃至你的母親與姐姐，我都不曾向他們提起究竟是什麼原因讓我放逐了你的哥哥。我原打算在自己離開這個世界之前，才告訴將要接掌先知之位的你；但上天的神明似乎再一次更改了我的計畫——敵人女祭司的自焚而亡，讓我迫切地意識到：孩子，你最好還是早點知曉這段隱秘的歷史。先知： 沒有甚麼事情能真正瞞得過你早慧的兄長，正如族中沒有甚麼事能瞞得過我一樣。身為先知，即便不與神明直接溝通，也擁有遠比常人敏銳的洞察力。你的兄長僅憑我的種種態度，便推斷出對方的女祭司毫不遜色於他的事實。單就這一點而言，族中那些只會死記硬背先知律法的長老們，甚至未曾察覺到半點端倪。你的兄長在年幼時便早已超越了他們，而他們卻只以為你的兄長是另一個我，全然不知先知與先知之間的差距，比先知與凡人的差距還要巨大——你的兄長，比作為父親的我更接近神明。先知： 人們知曉橋樑的存在，卻對橋樑上不同位置的意涵不甚了解；而這其實也不是他們所需要理解的事情。不同的人有著不同的命運，這都是神明所裁定的安排。先知： 你的兄長在某個夜晚，問了我幾個問題——正是那幾個問題，促使我做出了放逐他的決定。長子： 父親，那個女孩，是否並不遜色於我？先知： 孩子，有時連作為父親的我都感到你過於聰慧。你從未見過她，又是如何察覺到這一點的？長子： 父親，您未曾真正向我隱瞞過她的存在。先知沉默著，等待長子的下一個問題。他知道長子心中還有其他疑問。長子： 父親，我心中有些埋藏已久的疑問，今日我鼓起勇氣向您請教。先知： 你問吧，孩子。長子： 父親，您覺得那個女孩所侍奉的，究竟是一位偽神，還是一位真正的神明？先知沉默了，對長子問出這個問題感到十分意外。先知： 孩子，這個問題我此刻不能回答你。長子： 父親，我們身為先知家族，侍奉至高真神已有多年。如果那位女孩所侍奉的是偽神，為何她能不遜色於我？如果那位女孩所侍奉的是真神，那我未來又該如何面對她？先知： 孩子，對於族中事務，你所知曉的並不比我少，許多事情我也未曾瞞你。若非你年紀尚輕，長老們對你過多介入族務頗有微詞，我本會讓你接管更多。你心裡清楚，我們族人與她的族人絕無和解的可能——未來不是我們擊敗他們，就是他們擊敗我們；不是我們淪為俘虜，就是他們淪為階下之囚。長子： 我明白，父親。先知： 那麼，你是怎麼想的？長子： 我還不知道，父親。先知： 孩子，你不能不知道！你是族中未來的先知，甚至比作為父親的我更適合成為先知！有些問題一旦你問了出口，你就必須知曉相應的答案！長子： 父親，但我的心中浮現出了許多個可能的答案。先知： 你必須記住，你是族人的先知，你的答案只能有一個。長子： 父親，您認為答案應該是什麼？先知： 敵人的女祭司侍奉的是一位偽神；即便不是偽神，也是位格遠低於我們真神的次等神明。我們的族人、我們的戰士，只需要知道這個答案。長子： 父親，我們的族人與戰士，或許只是想要這個答案由我們家族的口中說出罷了。先知： 你越界了，孩子。長子： 對不起，父親。先知： 我們是族人的先知，這是我們必須時刻銘記的信條。你還有甚麼問題？那位被寄予厚望的英俊長子猶豫了片刻，還是問了出來。長子： 父親，還有一個問題我同樣思索了許久。我想知道……有沒有一種可能，我們所侍奉的神明，與她所侍奉的神明，其實是同一位神明？先知： 這絕不是你該問的問題！長子： 對不起，父親。我知道今晚過後我將失去您所有的信任，但我還有最後一個問題：神明對我們之間的這場戰爭，究竟有何看法？父親彷彿一下子蒼老了十歲。先知： 孩子……我的孩子……我們只是先知，我們只是橋樑 (γέφυρα = pons = bridge)。我們無法真正洞悉神明的全部旨意，也無法時刻捕捉到神明哪怕片段的意向。這一點，你早已明瞭了，是嗎？長子朝父親雙膝跪地，深深地行了一禮，淚流不止地離開了神廟。次子聽著父親的回憶，面無血色，蒼白到了極點。他深深地震驚於父親的話語，無法想像自己敬愛的兄長竟會問出這些他連想都不敢想的問題，更震驚於父親當時的應對態度。先知： 你的兄長問出了在他這個年紀不該問出的問題；他問出了唯有在他真正成為族中大先知時，才應當思索的問題。你的兄長……他實在太聰慧了。先知： 在你母親懷第一胎時，我曾向真神虔誠祈求，賜予我一個世上最具智慧的孩子。族中沉積多年的許多問題，連我這個先知都探尋不到更深層的答案，因此我祈求神明賜我一個孩子，去解決那些我無力化解的難題。你的兄長降生了，神明真的回應了我這名忠誠僕人的懇求，而你兄長的早慧，甚至遠遠超出了我的預期。先知： 你的兄長極喜愛算術、幾何、音樂與天文，我為他延請了最出色的導師。孩子，你還記得嗎？你兄長身邊總跟著一個亦僕亦友的大個子，那是族中從小培養來保護你兄長的死士。兄長閒暇時還會將學到的知識教給這位最親密的朋友，可惜那大個子有時連自己的名字都會寫錯。先知： 你兄長的學問，族中本就沒有多少人能懂。他受眾人愛戴，但同時又是無比孤獨的。命運女神的幽默在於，我們宿敵的女祭司，很可能是世上唯一能在這些學問上與你兄長交流的人。先知： 你兄長時常違背我的禁令，讓大個子偷偷帶些零食給你，這些我其實全都知道。先知： 我們出身於少數能繼承先知能力的神明祭司家族，絕不能沉迷於多餘的享樂，不能沉溺於肉體與物質的歡愉——美食、美色、名聲、財富以及放縱的享樂，皆不可成為我們的追求，因為我們必須成為神人之間的橋樑。先知： 這是成為先知的必經修煉。你的兄長隨身帶著零食，是因為他比家族中的大多數人都更超脫；他在幼年時就已不會沉迷於任何形式的物質享受，他的樂趣在於思索更高深的問題，他永遠在推演著旁人無法意識到其重要性的事物。任何零食糖果對他而言都可有可無，不過是生活裡無傷大雅的點綴。先知： 但孩子，你遠不如你的兄長那般克制，當初可是花了很大力氣，才學會不在零食面前哭鬧。先知： 當年你的兄長本該繼承一切，他疼愛你，覺得我把你也當作先知來培養是扼殺了你的天性與命運，這才吩咐那個亦僕亦友的大個子偷偷給你帶零食。先知： 但我們家族終究也只是先知，作為父親的我，更稱不上是在這條道路上走得最遠的人。我未能料到你的兄長竟寧願為了那幾個問題放棄一切——他愧疚於辜負了我這個父親的期望，愧疚於給家族帶來的巨大震撼，更愧疚於要由你來替他背負本不該屬於你的沉重宿命。先知： 孩子……成為先知本非你的宿命，但我們家族中已無人比你更合適；更可怕的是，在其他祭司家族之中，同樣找不出勝任之人。比你聰明的缺乏克制，比你節制的缺少勇氣，而在某些方面略勝你一籌的，又大多心術不正，根本無法承受作為神聖橋樑的重責大任。先知： 你與那個剛剛死去的女孩一樣，都背負了原本不屬於你們的宿命；問題在於，她比你更具備成為先知的天賦。我們這一代戰勝了他們，奴役了他們的族人，但我們族人的下一代又該何去何從？孩子，你必須提前知曉一些本不該在此刻得知的隱秘，因為為父也已別無他法了。先知： 我為何要放逐你的兄長？因為我清楚地預見到：倘若你的兄長依循他的理念成為先知，族中必將迎來一場前所未有的大動盪。我們傳統的律法在條文上或許不會被改動，但對其作出的全新詮釋，足以讓許多你所熟知的祭司長老陷入瘋狂；我們的族人亦將有大批無所適從，深陷難以自拔的迷茫之中。先知： 你的兄長甚至不需要刻意做出甚麼大動作，他僅僅是存在著、呼吸著，就能在潛移默化中重塑周遭的一切。那個大個子連字都寫不全，但在你兄長的影響下，卻時常捲入莫名其妙的爭鬥之中。先知： 許多長老至今仍不明白那些微小的衝突意味著甚麼，只當那是年輕人精力過剩的衝動，算不上甚麼大事；但我明白，那是未來一場毀滅性大地震確鑿無疑的前兆。先知： 孩子啊！你的兄長將會給族群帶來難以估量的毀滅！那些仍在暗中盤算權謀、搞小動作、為私利鑽營的長老與祭司們，對此依然一無所知。你的兄長待他們依然恭敬有加，但他們全然不知，他將給他們帶來根本無法想像的顛覆！族中許多人無比愛戴你的兄長，可他們同樣不知道，你的兄長究竟會為他們帶來甚麼！先知： 這些族人中，有許多是我兒時的玩伴。雖然隨著歲月流逝，我們彼此漸行漸遠，甚至有些人暗中與我為敵，但我絕無法眼睜睜看著他們被我的兒子毀滅，更無法放任族人跟隨你的兄長在精神世界中顛沛流離。我在婚禮上祝福過他們，看著他們的孩子長大成人，我深知他們每一家在戰場上犧牲過哪些親人；他們或許未曾察覺到我的目光，但我一直默默注視著他們，守護著他們。先知： 有些長老因我放逐了你的兄長而暗自竊喜，以為自己的家族有了更大的機會成為下一代先知；他們之中有些人，甚至連身上華美的祭司袍都捨不得脫下。先知： 聽，他們此刻正在狂歡。我們的族人被他們慷慨激昂的演講所打動，深信這場勝利再次印證了我們的律法承自真神，我們始終受真神庇佑。然而在他們之中，又有幾人真正懂得律法的真意？連我身為先知，解讀律法時都必須謹小慎微，有些長老卻以為只要將律法倒背如流，就是一名合格的祭司。先知： 無論命運如何安排，我們終究只是必有一死的凡人 (βροτός, θνητός = mortal)，先知亦不例外——凡人絕不可能完全知曉神明的全部旨意。先知： 孩子，那個女孩的家族曾經也是素負盛名的先知世家，我們的敵人亦曾盛極一時。他們後來多行不義，觸怒了神明，最終無法戰勝在德性上勝過他們的我們。然而，身為勝利者的我們，難道就真的比他們更接近永恆 (Αἰών = Aeon, Eternity)？先知： 有一個流傳已久的神話，傳說我們兩族的祖先當年都得到了眾神遺落人間的寶石，這才得以興起。不論這個神話究竟有幾分成真，今日對方一族已滅，但我們一族在未來又是否會重蹈他們的覆轍？先知： 你的兄長離開之後，未曾親手寄回過一封信。我所知曉的最後消息，來自那個在族中人人嘲笑其愚笨、只懂打架的大個子。他寫了一封滿是語法 (γραμματική = grammar) 與用詞錯誤的信，信中說他們即將渡過大海，往後恐怕難以再寄回任何音訊；他向故土的我們致意問候，叮囑我們要多保重，並祈願神明保佑一切安好。先知： 有時我真後悔當年對你兄長說過「教導天生愚笨之人實屬浪費力氣」這句話；以至於到頭來，我這個做父親的，也只能收到這樣一封滿是拙劣錯誤的信件，而那就是你兄長留下的最後消息。神話上的美麗．第四部分A 說完那個關於先知與次子對話的神話，又喝了一口水。在 B 發表自己的感想前，不知甚麼時候靜靜站在一邊聆聽的 C 先開口了。C： 這真是個悲傷的故事。B： 悲傷？為甚麼你會覺得悲傷呢？我覺得這個神話故事挺有意思的，故事裡的先知和我出身的文化傳統的先知有些一致的地方，比如故事裡的先知會立法，故事裡的先知也會釋法，這和我所知的現實一樣，但同時也有些不太一致的地方；然而總的來說，我沒有感覺到一絲悲傷。C： 我也不知道為何我會有這種感知，不同的人對同一個神話總會有不同的感知，我認為這也是很自然的事，你覺得呢？B： 你說得對，我只是好奇你的悲傷從何而來。同時我也好奇，是不是你出身的文化傳統中，和我出身的文化傳統一樣有許多關於先知的傳說？你們的先知在過去也立下過大量的律法嗎？C： 在我所在的文化傳統中，先知是神明的祭司，他們有男有女，從古至今都地位尊崇。祭司們制定曆法、進行占卜、記錄歷史、塑造習俗、傳授知識，並向貴族們提供統治的意見，但他們並不掌握與律法相關的事務。更廣義地說，在我所在的文化裡，雖然不可否認祭司們對政治有重大的影響，但他們不太積極參與政治，他們也不積極為世俗生活立下各種法律。B： 這對我來說有點不可思議。在我的文化中，先知祭司階層和統治者沒有太大區別，我們文化的很多律法與習俗都是直接由先知立下，再由祭司維護與解釋；先知立下的律法等同於神明立下的律法，關係到衣食住行的方方面面，嚴重違反律法的族人會被監禁、逐出族群、甚至判處死刑。B 頓了一頓，似乎在回憶一些事情。B： 雖然這些古時由先知祭司立下的律法，有不少已不再被人們維護，或者對其的解釋有了很大的改變，但有一部分古時的律法至今仍在被我們的族群奉行。很巧的是，剛才那個神話中關於「屠宰動物必須令其迅速死亡以減輕痛苦」的律法，在我所在的文化傳統中也有，而且一直傳承至今。C： 你說的這些對我來說也是很有意思的事，我對觀察不同文化的習俗一直懷有興趣。B： 可不可以這樣說：在我的文化裡，先知祭司比貴族掌握更多的實權；而在你的文化裡，則是貴族比祭司掌握更多的實權？C： 雖然這略有簡化，因為在我的族群裡不少祭司同時也是貴族，但總的來說你判斷得沒錯。甚至有這樣一種情況：在我們的貴族政治鬥爭中，會有人刻意操作，將政敵推到某個空缺的祭司位置上，那樣就可以令對手遠離權力核心。B： 真是有趣！C： 歷史上也有過祭司重回權力核心的案例，但他們的名聲通常會受到極大的損害，因為他們違反了自己對神明的誓言。而在我所在的文化中，違反對神明的誓言是一件極不道德的事，也是一件極可恥的事。B： 我另外有一個很好奇的問題，希望這個問題不會冒犯到你：不知道你是否相信神明的存在？C： 這對我來說不會是一個冒犯的問題，我相信神明的存在。你呢？B： 我並不相信神明的存在。如果你早一點來，聽到我和這位神話愛好者的對話，就會知道我很難接受任何不能在感知中重現、不能被理性推論的事物；我是一個相信實證與科學的人。我一直很希望有人能用我未曾想到的方式證明神明的存在，但很可惜的是，至今我還未遇到這樣的人。C： 你是不相信神明的存在，還是不相信神明的存在能被證明呢？B： 或許我是後者，我不相信神明的存在能被證明。就這一點來說，我是一個不可知論者 (Agnostic)，認為神明的存在無法被證明，同時神明的不存在也無法被證明。在我看來，無論神明存在與否，都是無法被證明的。A： 噢，你說的話令我想起了我的一位工程師朋友。B： 哈！真巧，我的工作就是做工程的。怎麼？你這個神話愛好者想嘗試向我證明神明的存在嗎？我覺得你可以試一試，這一定很有趣，我十分期待。A： 我的朋友，如果我擁有能向他人證明神明存在與否的才能，我將會十分惶恐。在我看來，我並不配擁有這種才能；而且我害怕自己擁有這種才能後，會不可避免地陷入那種最可怕的傲慢 (ὕβρις = hubris) 之中，那將是最深遠的詛咒。我的朋友，請不要期待我能向你證明神明的存在，這個想法太令我害怕了。B 望望 C，再轉回頭望向 A。B： 你這個反應對我來說還真是新奇。為何你覺得能證明神明存在是最可怕的傲慢 (ὕβρις = hubris)？A： 更準確地說，認為「我有辦法令人相信神明的存在」，這才是可怕的傲慢 (ὕβρις = hubris)。B： 你能進一步解釋你的想法嗎？A： 或許「傲慢」這個詞無法完全表達我的意思。我心中的詞是希臘文 ὕβρις (hubris)。ὕβρις (hubris) 不是一種簡單的傲慢，它是對神明的僭越，是凡人認為自己比神明更能理解甚麼才是正確的，是凡人認為自己比神明更高明、甚至認為自己已超越了神明的那種傲慢。ὕβρις (hubris) 是一種最大的狂妄。B： 所以你解釋的這個詞，和你害怕自己擁有「證明神明存在的才能」有甚麼關聯呢？A： 我的朋友，我們先假設神明存在。如果神明存在，那祂從過去、現在乃至未來都一直存在。B： 然後呢？A： 然而在每一個時代，都有不相信神明的人。那麼，神明沒有做的事，我一個凡人又如何能做到呢？如果我擁有能證明神明存在的才能，如果我能用可複製、可重現的手段去證明神明的存在，這不是表明我比神明更有智慧，更知道如何去說服一個人感知到神明的存在嗎？這就是我之前提到的那個最大的傲慢 ὕβρις (hubris) 啊！凡人如何能做到神明沒做的事呢？B： 原來你是這個意思！但我想問你，如果神明存在，為甚麼神明要讓人感知不到祂的存在？這是一種惡作劇嗎？還是說，即使神明存在，但對凡人是否相信祂或祂們的存在也漠不關心？請你回答我。A： 我的朋友，我也想知道這個問題的深層答案，很可惜我也不知道啊！B： 如果神明存在，人們卻無法感知到神明的存在，這對我來說是一件很不合理的事；所以我認為神明不存在更加合理。但我之前已說過，我認為神明不存在也是無法被證明的，所以神明存在與否這件事本身是不可知的，這對我來說很合理。C： 我的朋友，你有屬於你的嚴謹邏輯。B 轉向 C。B： 這位朋友，不知道你的意見又是如何？C： 說實話，你的疑問在我心中同樣有過，而我對這些問題也沒有任何確切的答案。令我對神明的存在仍有信心的，其實是一些我所認識的人的存在。B： 一些人的存在令你相信神明的存在？C： 那不是甚麼很複雜的理由，純粹是我認識一些很好的人，他們大部分都相信神明的存在，他們都非常虔誠。對我來說，他們和天使差不多；既然他們在我眼中是小天使，那麼天使的背後一定是神明。B： 然而這並不是甚麼確鑿的證據，我想你也知道這一點。C 點頭肯定。B： 在我的生命中，也有一些很好的人，但他們有不少都是不可知論者，或者是無神論者。沒有他們的存在，很可能我早早就已經死去了。對我來說，他們也是我的「天使」，然而這些「天使」卻懷疑神明的存在。C： 你說的有你的道理，這只是我個人有限的經驗所形成的有限意見。不過有時我會想，既然我認識的這些「小天使」都相信神明，或許我們設想有一個神明的存在也不壞；起碼在我的文化中，不論是哪位神明，都導人向善。B： 你說的這些我無法同意。在我所在的文化中，神明也導人向善，但無論是過去還是現在，都有人以神明的名義犯下極大的罪行。他們雖稱自己相信神明，但他們並沒有向善！對此我還能以自己的親身經驗作證：相信神明存在的人會作惡，反而是不相信神明的人對我抱有善意！其他兩人看到 B 隱隱表露出憤怒的情緒，恐怕是剛才的對話勾起了 B 一些十分不快的回憶。B： 很抱歉，剛才我想起了一些已經過去很久的事。我以為我已經忘記了，但原來沒有，這些記憶至今仍然深深地影響著我。A： 我猜想，這些回憶是你不願相信神明存在的更深一層原因。B： 你說得沒錯。我不能理解為甚麼有人可以以神之名行醜陋之事，這令他們倍加面目可憎，正是他們的存在令我更加傾向於神明不存在！神明既然存在，為何容許他們這樣做？這對我來說完全不合理。B 留意到 A 欲言又止。B： 這位神話愛好者，你想說甚麼就說吧。難道你終於忍不住打破了你對傲慢的恐懼，想要說服我其實是錯的？A： 不是的，我的朋友。我沒有想說你是對還是錯，只是剛才我腦海中閃過一個疑問，但我又不知道該不該在這個時機問出來。B： 我想那又是一個奇怪的問題，你問吧。A： 為甚麼你覺得以神之名行惡事是醜陋的呢？為甚麼你認為那是不美麗的呢？B： 這不是很明顯的事嗎？他們做的事是醜陋的，那就是醜陋的。A： 美麗與不美麗，與他們是否宣稱相信神明無關？B： 當然無關！或者說，他們自稱相信神明這一點，令他們更加醜陋！令他們離美麗更遠！A 好像陷入了思考，沒有再說話。B： 你怎麼不說話了？A： 噢，抱歉，我走神了。B： 你這就問完了？A： 我還有一個問題，就是你是怎麼感知到他們是不美麗的呢？B： 就是一種噁心的感覺。A： 為甚麼你會有這種感知呢？B： 哈！我真不該問你還有沒有問題！B 忍不住笑了出來。B： 我怎麼知道自己為何有這種感知！反正我就是感知到一種噁心的感覺！你看看，我們有新的觀眾加入了，在等待你回憶那些奇怪的神話故事呢，別想你那些奇奇怪怪的問題了！A： 稍等我一下，我要把我剛才的問題記下來，我害怕我會忘記這些問題。B 望向 C，用眼神交流，傳達了「這真是一個奇怪的人」的意思。

entry.title: Mythos & Kallos · Part 19-20

link.title: Mythos & Kallos · Part 19-20

entry.content:
Mythos & Kallos · Part 19 · Moirai δ

A: Friend, why do you watch me as I eat my bread? Are there crumbs upon my face?

B: Forgive me — it is only that the way you eat bread, so slow and unhurried, in small bites and gentle chewing, somewhat resembles a friend of mine.

A: So that is it. This is the upbringing I received as a child. The elders said that one must not eat too quickly, for all food is the Grace of the Gods, and we must cherish and give thanks for what the Gods bestow.

B: You are still so traditional. Ha ha — this saying that all food is the bestowal of the Gods, I too heard plenty of it when I was small. Such words were usually taken up by elders to lecture their own children not to eat too fast and not to waste food. Does your culture also have rites like prayer before the meal and thanksgiving after it?

A: We have them as well.

B: It seems this phenomenon exists across different cultures. From childhood I was weary of such religious rites and customs, yet who could have imagined that once I had children of my own, I too could not help wanting to use roughly the same words to teach them — only I no longer tell my children that this is the Grace of the Gods, but tell them that this is grain which people toiled hard to grow, that many in this world still cannot eat their fill, and that it must not be wasted. At mealtimes I too ask my children to eat more slowly; I say that scientific research shows it is good for the body, and that if they wish to grow taller they should eat slowly.

A: Understandable.

B: And yet in truth, when I was small I did not really obey these restraints upon eating either. People do sometimes become the very thing they once despised. But another friend of mine was not so fortunate — the discipline at home was exceedingly severe, and there was no daring to violate any...

At this point B suddenly began to cough.

B: Forgive me...

A: It is nothing, friend.

B faintly heard a timbre resembling that of the viola d'amore.

B: What a coincidence.

A: What coincidence?

B: Nothing — only that this sound of strings has once again reminded me of certain things from the past.

A: What have you recalled, friend?

B laughed softly, as though speaking to oneself: On the journey of life, does not each person, more or less, encounter certain people whom they both love and hate? Tell me, why is this so? Why is the world like this?

A: Oh, friend, I do not understand it either. The friendship and affinity (Φιλία = philia = friendship, affection, love) and the conflict and strife (νεῖκος = neikos = strife, quarrel, discord) of this world are perhaps a secret of the Gods. Why have these things come to your mind, friend?

B: Ah, forgive me... I was only reminded of a friend. Let me call this friend V. V, T, and I have known one another since childhood.

B cleared a throat that still felt not quite right.

B: V is that friend I just mentioned, the one with the strict upbringing. V's father passed away very early, and V's mother demanded a great deal of V. Sometimes to be born into a distinguished house of renown is perhaps not necessarily a good thing; the whole vast weight of the family's expectations is pressed upon you, demanding that you make good on them.

A: Is V's family very famous in your country?

B: V's family is not merely famous in my country — V's family is itself a part of our people's history. Certain famous figures in our history came from this family or from its collateral branches. Only under the frequent wars and violent political upheavals of the modern age has it become "slightly ordinary" — though even this "ordinariness" is ordinary only within limits. Great houses and great clans are truly colossal things.

B took a sip of wine.

B: It sounds glamorous, but V's own household was merely a collateral branch within the whole clan. V's father died unexpectedly early; in life he was a mid-level official in the state apparatus. V's mother also came from the old nobility, a house of name. According to V, V's mother was originally not meant to marry V's father, who belonged to a collateral branch, but the line of V's maternal grandfather ran into certain economic difficulties because of war and sundry reasons, and in the end, after some twists and turns, V's mother "married beneath her" to V's father — a man of potential, yet not quite the most outstanding.

B still felt some discomfort in the throat.

B: Heavens, what am I saying? I hope all this is not boring you? Blame it on V, who in the old days poured the wretched affairs of that family into me without cease.

A: Not at all, my friend. To learn of the culture and history of other places is most interesting.

B: If you find it tedious, interrupt me. After drinking, sometimes even I do not know where my talk will wander.

T, V, and I each came from different family backgrounds; compared with them, I was born into a very ordinary family. Perhaps I am not grateful to religion, but I am grateful that the religious school I attended did indeed offer quite a few useful scholarships. Had I accepted certain of those scholarships back then, I might now be working within the Church — a pity that from childhood I was never devout; I could not go against my heart and believe in things I did not believe.

As for T, T was born into a cultured family; parents and grandparents alike were intellectuals. T's family was not very wealthy; the paternal side enjoyed a somewhat good reputation locally, while the name of the maternal family was connected with the ancient priests of our people — though now there are no longer any priests in our country.

V was the one among the three of us from the most substantial household. In V's home I saw for the first time in my life what an antique instrument was — an instrument that looked like a violin. V told me it was not called a violin, but a viola d'amore, some two to three hundred years old.

A: Viola d'amore?

B: Also called the soft-toned viola (柔音中提琴). It has a design called sympathetic strings; once the sympathetic strings are set into resonance, the viola d'amore gives forth a peculiar echoing timbre. A few passages of music here just now truly sounded rather like the voice this instrument produces.

A: So that is how it is.

B: V's mother was a person of very powerful aura. I think no one would wish to be fixed by her eyes. When I first went to V's home to play, I did not know this.

Friend, can you imagine — a child going happily to a good friend's home to play, only to be scrutinized from head to toe by the friend's mother, and then interrogated about how one's studies were going and what one's family circumstances were roughly like — what kind of experience is that?

Even at school I had never met so severe an elder! Heavens, from that day forward I understood why V cared about our homework even more than I did; with so strict a mother, V could not help but be afraid. And it was not only I who was frightened — that was the first time I saw V, whom no one at school failed to like, with legs trembling, while I was drenched in cold sweat. Fortunately T was there.

A: Why so?

B: Compared with V and me, who were praised daily by our teachers, T's grades at school in those days were not outstanding, but T loved reading strange and curious books of historical tales. I mentioned to you that the name T derives from a defeated general; this fondness for history began when T was very small.

A: Oh.

B: After I had been "quizzed" by V's mother as though facing the final and ultimate examination, it was T's turn. When "quizzed" by V's mother, T for some reason brought up certain figures of the past, and unlike my stammering answers, once T came upon a beloved subject the words flowed in an unbroken stream. V and I both went pale, thinking V's mother would be angered by such a digressive answer — yet unexpectedly V's mother simply listened quietly, and before long departed. V's mother even instructed the household servants to buy us some very delicious pastries.

V was utterly stunned.

A: How interesting.

B: Looking back after so many years, I too find it interesting. Yet if I could turn back time, and the me of then and the me of now were set in that scene once more, I would still feel the urge to flee. V's mother's aura was too strong, her presence too overwhelming — truly suffocating. I have always felt that even after growing up I never met anyone bearing so heavy a sense of oppression; perhaps this counts as a childhood shadow. I truly find it hard to imagine what V's childhood must have been. But do you know what T thought of V's mother?

A: What?

B: T said V's mother was an elder very easy to get along with, and said that never before had T eaten such delicious dessert — truly too delicious. My heavens, T is indeed a thick-nerved person lacking in perception; from childhood to adulthood this seems never truly to have changed. The circuitry of that brain is rather peculiar. Speaking of this, I recall a few more things about T. Friend, do you know what my parents' expectations of me were?

Seeing A's curious expression, B went on unprompted.

B: When I was still small, my family's greatest wish was that I might find a respectable job, establish a family and a livelihood, and pass this life in peace and contentment — that was all. They spent all their strength to send me into that fine religious school, hoping too that I would never again have to suffer the hardships they had suffered. Of course, as you see, I did not fail their expectations — I only failed their faith... never mind, let us not speak of that for now. And V, friend — what do you think V's mother's expectations of V were?

A: What were they?

B: To become an outstanding presence that draws every gaze, whom no one anywhere could ignore — that was the endpoint of all V's mother's discipline of V. And V achieved it, or in some measure accomplished it more brilliantly than V's mother ever imagined. V has now become a great celebrity; so long as V is not utterly alone, no one can ignore V's presence — heh, far too many admirers. Ah, what a headache. Let us not speak of this either for now. Friend, guess what T's family expected of T?

A: Oh, I cannot guess, friend.

B: Ha ha — T's family wanted T to pursue "freedom." That was the expectation laid upon T.

A: Freedom?

B: Yes, freedom. Sometimes V and I truly envied T. T's family placed no restrictions whatsoever upon T. I suspect T's laxity was not entirely a matter of temperament, but of the family's way. The three of us once fought a war of words over this — let me think, how should I put it.

And so B recalled an episode from when the three were still students.

B, unable to bear T's absentmindedness, grabbed T by the shoulders and shook hard.

B: Can you not take this seriously? You asked us here to help you catch up on your lessons, and you will not properly remember anything!

T, entirely oblivious to the irritation of B and V, kept twirling a pen and laughing.

T said to the two friends: But I truly cannot remember these things.

B: Is your brain not good? Hurry up and memorize!

T: My brain is not as good as yours.

B: Your brain is better than mine.

T: No, my brain is the worst — my grades are not as good as either of yours.

V: Stop shaking that idiot; shake any more and what little brain-matter remains will be shaken clean out.

T: See!

B: Why can you not put your heart into it? If you will not, what did you call us here for?

T: Sorry, but I truly cannot remember. How about we stop studying and do something else? Did I not mention to you before that I wanted to go to the seaside? How about the three of us make a plan?

V: I am going home. I still have to practice my instrument.

B: And I am off to my part-time job.

T: Do not be like that — could you truly bear to abandon your good friend of so many years?

B: I can bear it. You are not more important than my job.

V: You are simply too idle, and too free.

B: Right — no discipline. If you went into the army, you would be finished on the very first day.

T: I do have discipline, but I truly cannot remember. I have already tried very hard to remember; it is just that memory does not leave deep enough traces.

B stared at V and T.

B: You did not follow V to that drinking gathering yesterday, did you?

T: No.

V: Sigh — you two never come.

B: Are you not the darling of the multitudes? If we came we would fear stealing your limelight.

V: All I hear is the voice of envy. Honestly, it would be better with the two of you there.

B: Is socializing not your favorite thing?

T: Yes, yes, yes.

V: There is no talking with you two.

T: Yes, yes, yes.

B: Yes your head! Back to business! This truly is not hard to remember. You can recite obscure anecdotes of famous people and mathematical and physical equations by heart — do you think this history is harder to remember than those strange little hobbies of yours?

V: Leave T be. This one will behave once the course is failed.

T: This truly is not easy to remember.

This time it was V's turn to shake the still-laughing T.

T: I am dizzy.

V: Tell me honestly — where exactly do you find it hard to remember? Have we not already marked out all the key points for you?

B: Right — are the points we marked not eye-catching enough, not beautiful enough? Would you be satisfied only if we drew them in seven colors?

T: But I feel it is unreasonable.

B: Come, tell us — where is what we marked unreasonable?

T: No, it is not that what you marked is unreasonable; it is only that I feel something is a little unreasonable.

V and B looked somewhat displeased.

B: Speak! Tell us exactly what is unreasonable!

T: Do not be angry — I only feel that these few books have a few slightly unreasonable places.

V: What is unreasonable? Speak.

Then T spoke of a whole heap of places in the books that seemed unreasonable. At first B could still follow, but T's speech grew ever more circuitous, and by the end B had no idea at all what T was saying. B looked blankly toward V.

B saw only V frowning, that fine-featured face wearing a solemn expression.

V: Did you think all of these up yourself, T?

T: Just thoughts that wandered off while you were helping me study just now.

B: I said you were absentminded the whole time — admit it.

V turned T to face V.

V: Promise me — in the exam, never ever write these on the answer sheet, and in daily life never mention these ideas of yours to others.

T: Huh?

B: Did you understand what T just said?

V: Not entirely — about half of it.

T: Huh?

B: What on earth did T just say?

V: T is using some method learned from who knows where to "creatively" interpret history.

T: Huh?

V: Is this what your family taught you?

T: No, they only told me to pursue freedom.

B: What does this have to do with freedom? Free improvisation? Free interpretation?

Seeing the two good friends staring in silence, T finally felt embarrassed.

T: I am sorry, I did not think this would waste your time; I simply could not help having these thoughts.

V, however, was more earnest than B, and continued to question T.

V: This is related to freedom?

T: My grandfather told me that freedom is not disorder.

V: And so?

T: What is reasonable makes one free; what is ordered makes one free.

T nodded.

V: Is that so?

V fell silent for a good while, tapping the tabletop, as though pondering something.

B, seeing V unusually serious, did not interrupt V's thought.

V: As a good friend, I hope that from now on you tell these ideas only to the two of us. In exams, truly do not write like this, and do not tell anyone else. Promise me, will you?

T: Mm, alright.

V: I want you to promise me seriously.

T: A serious mm, a serious alright.

B: Then what about T's exam?

V: We shall speak of it once the course is failed.

T: Don't... save me.

V: No saving.

Recalling these things, B laughed softly.

B: Afterwards V truly paid T no more mind at all; it was I who later turned down my part-time work and secretly helped T catch up.

A: So did T pass that course in the end?

B: Failed, as expected. In the end it was V who somehow worked things so that the professor gave T a pass — otherwise T would have had a hard time of it.

A: The three of you truly share a close bond.

Yet a desolate expression came over B's face, the smile tinged with bitterness.

B: Yes indeed — long live friendship.

Through the window B gazed toward the nocturnal sea; all that met the eye was pitch darkness, and perhaps only by lending half the mind to the sound of the waves could one confirm that the sea still existed.

Mythos & Kallos · Part 20 · Moirai ε

B: Friend, in truth I have never liked the sea.

A: Why is that?

B: Perhaps it has to do with my having nearly died by drowning — ha ha — but the sea is indeed not a thing that invites fondness; I truly do not like the ocean. The sea is too vast; its depths cannot be fathomed; it has no direction whatsoever; it has no front or back, no left or right. Any creature of the land that stumbles into it is swallowed without mercy. The sea, to humankind, is in truth not friendly — would you not agree?

A: Understandable.

B: Even though people can build ships, a ship is but a small leaf adrift upon an infinite terror. A sea with no shore in sight may be more dreadful than a desert.

I have an elder who was a seafarer — my uncle, my mother's brother.

My uncle would sometimes tell me that someone he had long known had lost their mind at sea; that someone had sunk into depression and anxiety and fallen into strange delusions; that those who make their living on the far seas may harm themselves, or even take their own lives.

More terrible still, there were those who one day simply vanished from the ship, and however one searched, the person could not be found.

Perhaps suicide, perhaps murder —

and aboard the ship rumors might spread of wronged souls claiming their due, of possession by spirits and goblins, of foreign and wicked gods. Sounds like a horror tale, does it not?

B rubbed their nose.

B: Friend, to tell the truth, I sometimes suspect my uncle too had long since gone mad — only he did not show it very plainly.

I heard from my aunt that my uncle would at times sit quietly alone, staring into nothing, as though lacking a little of the breath of soul and life; no one knew what he was thinking.

Probably because my uncle had been rather close to me since I was small, there were certain matters of the sea he told only to me.

My uncle went to sea year after year to earn money, and my aunt needed only to manage the affairs of the household. She was a devout believer, actively taking part in the activities of the Church, which at times brought no small suffering upon my poor cousins.

To my aunt, the Gods not only exist — they must exist. Once, the ship my uncle sailed on suffered a grave accident in which people died, and my aunt held that it was her unceasing prayer that had taken effect — that the Gods had protected her man and protected her family. Throughout my uncle's long leave my aunt dragged him day after day to pray and give thanks to the Gods. My uncle found it tiresome, yet did not refuse his own wife.

Forgive me — am I perhaps saying too much and wearying you a little?

A: Not at all, my friend.

B: And so from childhood to adulthood I have never liked the sea. The seashore, to me, is no romantic fancy or holiday haven; it is a cold, dark, damp unknown devoid of humanity. Perhaps it bears you no malice, yet it holds absolutely no goodwill either — like a sleepwalking whale that, even as it slumbers, swallows into its belly the small fish and shrimp that pass by. It does not know you exist; your life and death are nothing to it.

Nor have I ever liked places such as aquariums. People always think that this jellyfish in the aquarium is so beautiful, that that fish never seen before is so marvelous.

But to me, the creatures of the aquarium seem to live in a world wholly parallel to that of humankind. Puppies and kittens and some land animals can respond to a person — but the creatures of the sea? Meeting a person, they either flee, or kill you, or poison you without even being aware of it. I truly cannot bring myself to admire them.

Is the ocean beautiful? Perhaps. But that is not a beauty in affinity with humankind.

A: Friend, hearing you speak reminds me of a story about the ocean.

B: Go on — I knew it was about time your craving for storytelling flared up.

And so A recalled a myth concerning the ocean.

Long, long ago,

people did not in fact live upon the land as they do now;

the people of the ancient age were amphibious lives (ἀμφίβιος = ἀμφί + βίος) —

waking, they lived upon the land;

dreaming, they slept submerged in the sea;

dwelling in no fixed place,

they migrated without cease across the world, following the monsoons and the ocean currents.

Other lives asked humankind:

O humans, you who thus roam the world without end,

going from one place to another —

for what reason do you do so?

The people of that time replied:

We envy and yearn to fly as the birds do;

that is the lullaby (καταβαυκάλησις = singing a lullaby) the Gods softly croon in our dreams.

The other lives asked:

Have the Gods said something to you?

The people answered:

The Gods said to us:

Embrace the sky (Οὐρανός = Ouranos = Sky, Heaven),

touch freedom (ἐλεύθερος = liberty, free),

newborn child (παῖς = child).

The other lives asked again:

How strange you humans are —

have you no place that belongs to you?

Have you no home?

The people wondered in perplexity:

Home? What is home?

In that age, the boundaries between life and death, between waking and dreaming, were blurred and indistinct.

For the people of that time,

one generation being born and another generation dying (Θάνατος = Thanatos = Death)

was simply one generation waking and another generation falling asleep (Ὕπνος = Hypnos = Sleep).

People lived amphibiously between land and sea;

people lived amphibiously between waking and dream (ὄνειρος = Oneiros = Dream);

people could not tell what difference lay between the two, nor did they seek to.

The chance and the necessity met with while waking,

the chance and the necessity met with in dream —

there was no difference between them.

And so it was:

generation upon generation blossomed,

generation upon generation withered;

while waking, some would ponder what home is,

and in dream, some too would pursue the question of what home is.

Generation after generation, for who knows how long,

this question became an unsleeping echo (Ἠχώ = Echo) between the generations.

Because of this attention to and curiosity about "home,"

people, without being aware of it,

began in their dreams to pray to the Gods, asking what "home" is.

Devout prayer condensed into the supplications of each person,

and these supplications, great and small, embraced one another,

gathering into an expedition,

from the shallow sea to the deep sea,

from faint glimmering light into darkness,

in the icy waters of the sea,

searching for that legendary abyss (ἄβυσσος = abyss, bottomless depth) whose bottom cannot be seen —

where, it was said, the God who truly rules the ocean dwells.

When the people awoke,

they forgot the prayers to which they had given breath in dream.

They had only a faint impression,

as though they had asked some question.

The stars revolved,

and after who knows how long,

a new legend circulated in the dreams of the people.

That rumor, never heard before, said

that a beautiful white bull had been born from the farthest end of the deep sea.

And then more and more people said they had seen that legendary white bull.

"Oh! So the white bull is truly real!"

And so those who discovered the white bull in the sea followed behind that miraculous creature,

and new witnesses joined without cease this ever-swelling procession brimming with curiosity.

The people wished to see

where the beautiful white bull truly wished to go,

and whether it had a final destination (τέλος = telos = end, destination, fulfillment).

Someone could not help asking the white bull:

Beautiful white bull, where are you really going? Are you searching for something?

The white bull said:

I dreamed of a beautiful seven-colored rainbow (Ἶρις = Iris = Rainbow);

in the dream, the rainbow in the vault of heaven was singing to me.

The people asked again:

So you wish to find the rainbow in the sky —

but we cannot fly; when the time comes, may we still follow you?

The white bull said:

I do not know either.

The people who shared the dream with the white bull asked no more, and continued silently to follow.

Without clamor or commotion, like an orderly school of fish,

they circled the luminous white bull, swimming back and forth in regular rhythm.

Light and shadow alternated,

and after who knows how long,

the white bull said it heard a tremendous sound.

Slowly it swam upward,

leaving the deep sea,

leaving the shallow sea,

at last breaking free of the surface,

and breathing the air of the land.

The multitude of people followed the white bull onto the shore,

and they saw, upon the earth beneath a torrential storm, a dreadful and enormous rift (χάσμα = chasma = chasm, rift, gulf),

as though struck by a lightning never seen before,

the flames it left behind not extinguished even beneath the falling drops of rain.

At this moment the white bull seemed to lose all its strength;

it knelt upon all four legs, its breathing ever thinner.

The people asked it:

What is wrong? Are you ill? Should we return to the sea?

The white bull answered:

Thank you,

but I think I shall soon die;

my life is ebbing away without cease.

Perhaps this is my end (τέλος = telos = end, destination, fulfillment).

The people asked:

But what of the rainbow?

Did you not say you would find the rainbow?

We have not yet seen the rainbow.

The white bull said:

Dear friends,

I can still hear the song of the rainbow (ᾠδή = ode = song, ode).

Perhaps the final stretch of the road cannot be reached by the body.

Could you deliver me to the rainbow's side?

This is a pact.

The people asked:

What must we do?

The white bull said:

Have your leader of song adorn me;

we shall bathe together in pure clean water;

then lay gold leaf upon my great horns,

and set my strengthless body amid fragrant wood.

The people asked:

Is that all that is needed?

The white bull said:

Oh —

have your leader of song, amid singing and dancing,

take up that flame which does not go out beneath the rain,

and set me alight together with the fragrant wood.

I shall become formless smoke and fire,

and under the witness of the Gods,

bearing our hopes with me, I shall behold the rainbow.

Please consent to this oath (ὅρκος = oath, sworn pledge) between us,

my best friends, faithful companions on the journey of my life.

The people asked:

But, if that is so, you will die.

The white bull said:

Dear friends,

I have been away from home too long;

I too must return home.

Please promise me

that once I have become smoke,

you will share and eat my flesh and blood;

this shall become our common memory,

a mark passed down through the generations.

And the bones I leave behind,

and those horns touched with gold leaf —

please, by no means take them away;

arrange them into a fine and pleasing form,

and let them sink beneath that rift into the waters of the sea.

My soul shall follow them home (νόστος = nostos = homecoming, return).

The people did not understand:

Home? What is home?

What kind of place is it?

The white bull said:

Do you not know?

The people answered:

We do not know.

The white bull said:

Then please bind the longest rope in the world to my white bones;

when the rope falls wholly still,

you will know that I have returned home.

The people asked again:

Then what is home?

The white bull answered:

Dear friends,

returning home and home are different ways of speaking of one and the same thing.

So long as you feel the rope fall wholly still,

in the moment you know I have returned home,

you too will surely understand what home is.

The people asked once more:

And what of us?

When you have died, where should we go?

The white bull said:

I do not know either.

Perhaps, after I have returned home,

you might wait and see whether the rainbow appears in the sky,

pray to the Gods,

and then consider where you wish to go.

I am sorry

that I cannot bring you to behold the true rainbow (Ἶρις = Iris = Rainbow),

nor invite you back to the place where my dream began.

If you should miss me,

you may look upon and touch that rope;

it is the gravestone and symbol of my rest (σῆμα = sema = sign, mark, tomb, monument),

it is the memory in which I and you still take part (μνήμη = mneme = memory, remembrance),

and it is the miracle promised by the Gods (θαῦμα = thauma = wonder, marvel).

May the Gods protect you.

Weeping and laughing,

the people, as promised, burned the white bull amid the fragrant wood.

The white bull neither suffered nor cried out;

only, seeing the people weep for it,

it too shed its final tears.

A great fire never seen before

drove away the darkness and the cold.

From the still-blazing flames,

the people carefully drew forth the white bones the white bull had left behind.

The gold leaf upon the horns had not fallen away,

but had instead fused into the whole pair of horns,

granting them the radiance of pure gold.

The other peoples wandering the world,

seeing from afar the vast flame,

became the final participants in this rite of sacrifice;

they were invited to witness (μάρτυς = martyr = witness)

how the bones of the white bull sank back through the rift into the deep sea.

The people saw

that the longest rope in the world,

like a fish drawn out of water,

trembled without cease in the dryness,

giving forth a sound at every moment,

never resting, day after day and night after night.

Sun and moon rose and set,

life and death turned in their cycle,

and no one knows how long again passed —

several generations, perhaps? Or perhaps more than ten?

Beneath the oath,

that rope, already become legend, was still kept watch over by the people.

Until one dawn, when most were still asleep in dream,

the rope suddenly gave forth no more sound,

and fell still.

The people, who had long since bid farewell to the amphibious life

and no longer entered dream within the sea,

gazed upon the faint rainbow of the dawn,

embracing one another, trembling,

and in accordance with the final pact with the white bull,

named in remembrance its unseen relic at the far end

anchor (ἄγκυρα = anchor).

That was the people's final memory of the white bull.
entry.summary: Mythos & Kallos · Part 19 · Moirai δA: Friend, why do you watch me as I eat my bread? Are there crumbs upon my face?B: Forgive me — it is only that the way you eat bread, so slow and unhurried, in small bites and gentle chewing, somewhat resembles a friend of mine.A: So that is it. This is the upbringing I received as a child. The elders said that one must not eat too quickly, for all food is the Grace of the Gods, and we must cherish and give thanks for what the Gods bestow.B: You are still so traditional. Ha ha — this saying that all food is the bestowal of the Gods, I too heard plenty of it when I was small. Such words were usually taken up by elders to lecture their own children not to eat too fast and not to waste food. Does your culture also have rites like prayer before the meal and thanksgiving after it?A: We have them as well.B: It seems this phenomenon exists across different cultures. From childhood I was weary of such religious rites and customs, yet who could have imagined that once I had children of my own, I too could not help wanting to use roughly the same words to teach them — only I no longer tell my children that this is the Grace of the Gods, but tell them that this is grain which people toiled hard to grow, that many in this world still cannot eat their fill, and that it must not be wasted. At mealtimes I too ask my children to eat more slowly; I say that scientific research shows it is good for the body, and that if they wish to grow taller they should eat slowly.A: Understandable.B: And yet in truth, when I was small I did not really obey these restraints upon eating either. People do sometimes become the very thing they once despised. But another friend of mine was not so fortunate — the discipline at home was exceedingly severe, and there was no daring to violate any...At this point B suddenly began to cough.B: Forgive me...A: It is nothing, friend.B faintly heard a timbre resembling that of the viola d'amore.B: What a coincidence.A: What coincidence?B: Nothing — only that this sound of strings has once again reminded me of certain things from the past.A: What have you recalled, friend?B laughed softly, as though speaking to oneself: On the journey of life, does not each person, more or less, encounter certain people whom they both love and hate? Tell me, why is this so? Why is the world like this?A: Oh, friend, I do not understand it either. The friendship and affinity (Φιλία = philia = friendship, affection, love) and the conflict and strife (νεῖκος = neikos = strife, quarrel, discord) of this world are perhaps a secret of the Gods. Why have these things come to your mind, friend?B: Ah, forgive me... I was only reminded of a friend. Let me call this friend V. V, T, and I have known one another since childhood.B cleared a throat that still felt not quite right.B: V is that friend I just mentioned, the one with the strict upbringing. V's father passed away very early, and V's mother demanded a great deal of V. Sometimes to be born into a distinguished house of renown is perhaps not necessarily a good thing; the whole vast weight of the family's expectations is pressed upon you, demanding that you make good on them.A: Is V's family very famous in your country?B: V's family is not merely famous in my country — V's family is itself a part of our people's history. Certain famous figures in our history came from this family or from its collateral branches. Only under the frequent wars and violent political upheavals of the modern age has it become "slightly ordinary" — though even this "ordinariness" is ordinary only within limits. Great houses and great clans are truly colossal things.B took a sip of wine.B: It sounds glamorous, but V's own household was merely a collateral branch within the whole clan. V's father died unexpectedly early; in life he was a mid-level official in the state apparatus. V's mother also came from the old nobility, a house of name. According to V, V's mother was originally not meant to marry V's father, who belonged to a collateral branch, but the line of V's maternal grandfather ran into certain economic difficulties because of war and sundry reasons, and in the end, after some twists and turns, V's mother "married beneath her" to V's father — a man of potential, yet not quite the most outstanding.B still felt some discomfort in the throat.B: Heavens, what am I saying? I hope all this is not boring you? Blame it on V, who in the old days poured the wretched affairs of that family into me without cease.A: Not at all, my friend. To learn of the culture and history of other places is most interesting.B: If you find it tedious, interrupt me. After drinking, sometimes even I do not know where my talk will wander.T, V, and I each came from different family backgrounds; compared with them, I was born into a very ordinary family. Perhaps I am not grateful to religion, but I am grateful that the religious school I attended did indeed offer quite a few useful scholarships. Had I accepted certain of those scholarships back then, I might now be working within the Church — a pity that from childhood I was never devout; I could not go against my heart and believe in things I did not believe.As for T, T was born into a cultured family; parents and grandparents alike were intellectuals. T's family was not very wealthy; the paternal side enjoyed a somewhat good reputation locally, while the name of the maternal family was connected with the ancient priests of our people — though now there are no longer any priests in our country.V was the one among the three of us from the most substantial household. In V's home I saw for the first time in my life what an antique instrument was — an instrument that looked like a violin. V told me it was not called a violin, but a viola d'amore, some two to three hundred years old.A: Viola d'amore?B: Also called the soft-toned viola (柔音中提琴). It has a design called sympathetic strings; once the sympathetic strings are set into resonance, the viola d'amore gives forth a peculiar echoing timbre. A few passages of music here just now truly sounded rather like the voice this instrument produces.A: So that is how it is.B: V's mother was a person of very powerful aura. I think no one would wish to be fixed by her eyes. When I first went to V's home to play, I did not know this.Friend, can you imagine — a child going happily to a good friend's home to play, only to be scrutinized from head to toe by the friend's mother, and then interrogated about how one's studies were going and what one's family circumstances were roughly like — what kind of experience is that?Even at school I had never met so severe an elder! Heavens, from that day forward I understood why V cared about our homework even more than I did; with so strict a mother, V could not help but be afraid. And it was not only I who was frightened — that was the first time I saw V, whom no one at school failed to like, with legs trembling, while I was drenched in cold sweat. Fortunately T was there.A: Why so?B: Compared with V and me, who were praised daily by our teachers, T's grades at school in those days were not outstanding, but T loved reading strange and curious books of historical tales. I mentioned to you that the name T derives from a defeated general; this fondness for history began when T was very small.A: Oh.B: After I had been "quizzed" by V's mother as though facing the final and ultimate examination, it was T's turn. When "quizzed" by V's mother, T for some reason brought up certain figures of the past, and unlike my stammering answers, once T came upon a beloved subject the words flowed in an unbroken stream. V and I both went pale, thinking V's mother would be angered by such a digressive answer — yet unexpectedly V's mother simply listened quietly, and before long departed. V's mother even instructed the household servants to buy us some very delicious pastries.V was utterly stunned.A: How interesting.B: Looking back after so many years, I too find it interesting. Yet if I could turn back time, and the me of then and the me of now were set in that scene once more, I would still feel the urge to flee. V's mother's aura was too strong, her presence too overwhelming — truly suffocating. I have always felt that even after growing up I never met anyone bearing so heavy a sense of oppression; perhaps this counts as a childhood shadow. I truly find it hard to imagine what V's childhood must have been. But do you know what T thought of V's mother?A: What?B: T said V's mother was an elder very easy to get along with, and said that never before had T eaten such delicious dessert — truly too delicious. My heavens, T is indeed a thick-nerved person lacking in perception; from childhood to adulthood this seems never truly to have changed. The circuitry of that brain is rather peculiar. Speaking of this, I recall a few more things about T. Friend, do you know what my parents' expectations of me were?Seeing A's curious expression, B went on unprompted.B: When I was still small, my family's greatest wish was that I might find a respectable job, establish a family and a livelihood, and pass this life in peace and contentment — that was all. They spent all their strength to send me into that fine religious school, hoping too that I would never again have to suffer the hardships they had suffered. Of course, as you see, I did not fail their expectations — I only failed their faith... never mind, let us not speak of that for now. And V, friend — what do you think V's mother's expectations of V were?A: What were they?B: To become an outstanding presence that draws every gaze, whom no one anywhere could ignore — that was the endpoint of all V's mother's discipline of V. And V achieved it, or in some measure accomplished it more brilliantly than V's mother ever imagined. V has now become a great celebrity; so long as V is not utterly alone, no one can ignore V's presence — heh, far too many admirers. Ah, what a headache. Let us not speak of this either for now. Friend, guess what T's family expected of T?A: Oh, I cannot guess, friend.B: Ha ha — T's family wanted T to pursue "freedom." That was the expectation laid upon T.A: Freedom?B: Yes, freedom. Sometimes V and I truly envied T. T's family placed no restrictions whatsoever upon T. I suspect T's laxity was not entirely a matter of temperament, but of the family's way. The three of us once fought a war of words over this — let me think, how should I put it.And so B recalled an episode from when the three were still students.B, unable to bear T's absentmindedness, grabbed T by the shoulders and shook hard.B: Can you not take this seriously? You asked us here to help you catch up on your lessons, and you will not properly remember anything!T, entirely oblivious to the irritation of B and V, kept twirling a pen and laughing.T said to the two friends: But I truly cannot remember these things.B: Is your brain not good? Hurry up and memorize!T: My brain is not as good as yours.B: Your brain is better than mine.T: No, my brain is the worst — my grades are not as good as either of yours.V: Stop shaking that idiot; shake any more and what little brain-matter remains will be shaken clean out.T: See!B: Why can you not put your heart into it? If you will not, what did you call us here for?T: Sorry, but I truly cannot remember. How about we stop studying and do something else? Did I not mention to you before that I wanted to go to the seaside? How about the three of us make a plan?V: I am going home. I still have to practice my instrument.B: And I am off to my part-time job.T: Do not be like that — could you truly bear to abandon your good friend of so many years?B: I can bear it. You are not more important than my job.V: You are simply too idle, and too free.B: Right — no discipline. If you went into the army, you would be finished on the very first day.T: I do have discipline, but I truly cannot remember. I have already tried very hard to remember; it is just that memory does not leave deep enough traces.B stared at V and T.B: You did not follow V to that drinking gathering yesterday, did you?T: No.V: Sigh — you two never come.B: Are you not the darling of the multitudes? If we came we would fear stealing your limelight.V: All I hear is the voice of envy. Honestly, it would be better with the two of you there.B: Is socializing not your favorite thing?T: Yes, yes, yes.V: There is no talking with you two.T: Yes, yes, yes.B: Yes your head! Back to business! This truly is not hard to remember. You can recite obscure anecdotes of famous people and mathematical and physical equations by heart — do you think this history is harder to remember than those strange little hobbies of yours?V: Leave T be. This one will behave once the course is failed.T: This truly is not easy to remember.This time it was V's turn to shake the still-laughing T.T: I am dizzy.V: Tell me honestly — where exactly do you find it hard to remember? Have we not already marked out all the key points for you?B: Right — are the points we marked not eye-catching enough, not beautiful enough? Would you be satisfied only if we drew them in seven colors?T: But I feel it is unreasonable.B: Come, tell us — where is what we marked unreasonable?T: No, it is not that what you marked is unreasonable; it is only that I feel something is a little unreasonable.V and B looked somewhat displeased.B: Speak! Tell us exactly what is unreasonable!T: Do not be angry — I only feel that these few books have a few slightly unreasonable places.V: What is unreasonable? Speak.Then T spoke of a whole heap of places in the books that seemed unreasonable. At first B could still follow, but T's speech grew ever more circuitous, and by the end B had no idea at all what T was saying. B looked blankly toward V.B saw only V frowning, that fine-featured face wearing a solemn expression.V: Did you think all of these up yourself, T?T: Just thoughts that wandered off while you were helping me study just now.B: I said you were absentminded the whole time — admit it.V turned T to face V.V: Promise me — in the exam, never ever write these on the answer sheet, and in daily life never mention these ideas of yours to others.T: Huh?B: Did you understand what T just said?V: Not entirely — about half of it.T: Huh?B: What on earth did T just say?V: T is using some method learned from who knows where to "creatively" interpret history.T: Huh?V: Is this what your family taught you?T: No, they only told me to pursue freedom.B: What does this have to do with freedom? Free improvisation? Free interpretation?Seeing the two good friends staring in silence, T finally felt embarrassed.T: I am sorry, I did not think this would waste your time; I simply could not help having these thoughts.V, however, was more earnest than B, and continued to question T.V: This is related to freedom?T: My grandfather told me that freedom is not disorder.V: And so?T: What is reasonable makes one free; what is ordered makes one free.T nodded.V: Is that so?V fell silent for a good while, tapping the tabletop, as though pondering something.B, seeing V unusually serious, did not interrupt V's thought.V: As a good friend, I hope that from now on you tell these ideas only to the two of us. In exams, truly do not write like this, and do not tell anyone else. Promise me, will you?T: Mm, alright.V: I want you to promise me seriously.T: A serious mm, a serious alright.B: Then what about T's exam?V: We shall speak of it once the course is failed.T: Don't... save me.V: No saving.Recalling these things, B laughed softly.B: Afterwards V truly paid T no more mind at all; it was I who later turned down my part-time work and secretly helped T catch up.A: So did T pass that course in the end?B: Failed, as expected. In the end it was V who somehow worked things so that the professor gave T a pass — otherwise T would have had a hard time of it.A: The three of you truly share a close bond.Yet a desolate expression came over B's face, the smile tinged with bitterness.B: Yes indeed — long live friendship.Through the window B gazed toward the nocturnal sea; all that met the eye was pitch darkness, and perhaps only by lending half the mind to the sound of the waves could one confirm that the sea still existed.Mythos & Kallos · Part 20 · Moirai εB: Friend, in truth I have never liked the sea.A: Why is that?B: Perhaps it has to do with my having nearly died by drowning — ha ha — but the sea is indeed not a thing that invites fondness; I truly do not like the ocean. The sea is too vast; its depths cannot be fathomed; it has no direction whatsoever; it has no front or back, no left or right. Any creature of the land that stumbles into it is swallowed without mercy. The sea, to humankind, is in truth not friendly — would you not agree?A: Understandable.B: Even though people can build ships, a ship is but a small leaf adrift upon an infinite terror. A sea with no shore in sight may be more dreadful than a desert.I have an elder who was a seafarer — my uncle, my mother's brother.My uncle would sometimes tell me that someone he had long known had lost their mind at sea; that someone had sunk into depression and anxiety and fallen into strange delusions; that those who make their living on the far seas may harm themselves, or even take their own lives.More terrible still, there were those who one day simply vanished from the ship, and however one searched, the person could not be found.Perhaps suicide, perhaps murder —and aboard the ship rumors might spread of wronged souls claiming their due, of possession by spirits and goblins, of foreign and wicked gods. Sounds like a horror tale, does it not?B rubbed their nose.B: Friend, to tell the truth, I sometimes suspect my uncle too had long since gone mad — only he did not show it very plainly.I heard from my aunt that my uncle would at times sit quietly alone, staring into nothing, as though lacking a little of the breath of soul and life; no one knew what he was thinking.Probably because my uncle had been rather close to me since I was small, there were certain matters of the sea he told only to me.My uncle went to sea year after year to earn money, and my aunt needed only to manage the affairs of the household. She was a devout believer, actively taking part in the activities of the Church, which at times brought no small suffering upon my poor cousins.To my aunt, the Gods not only exist — they must exist. Once, the ship my uncle sailed on suffered a grave accident in which people died, and my aunt held that it was her unceasing prayer that had taken effect — that the Gods had protected her man and protected her family. Throughout my uncle's long leave my aunt dragged him day after day to pray and give thanks to the Gods. My uncle found it tiresome, yet did not refuse his own wife.Forgive me — am I perhaps saying too much and wearying you a little?A: Not at all, my friend.B: And so from childhood to adulthood I have never liked the sea. The seashore, to me, is no romantic fancy or holiday haven; it is a cold, dark, damp unknown devoid of humanity. Perhaps it bears you no malice, yet it holds absolutely no goodwill either — like a sleepwalking whale that, even as it slumbers, swallows into its belly the small fish and shrimp that pass by. It does not know you exist; your life and death are nothing to it.Nor have I ever liked places such as aquariums. People always think that this jellyfish in the aquarium is so beautiful, that that fish never seen before is so marvelous.But to me, the creatures of the aquarium seem to live in a world wholly parallel to that of humankind. Puppies and kittens and some land animals can respond to a person — but the creatures of the sea? Meeting a person, they either flee, or kill you, or poison you without even being aware of it. I truly cannot bring myself to admire them.Is the ocean beautiful? Perhaps. But that is not a beauty in affinity with humankind.A: Friend, hearing you speak reminds me of a story about the ocean.B: Go on — I knew it was about time your craving for storytelling flared up.And so A recalled a myth concerning the ocean.Long, long ago,people did not in fact live upon the land as they do now;the people of the ancient age were amphibious lives (ἀμφίβιος = ἀμφί + βίος) —waking, they lived upon the land;dreaming, they slept submerged in the sea;dwelling in no fixed place,they migrated without cease across the world, following the monsoons and the ocean currents.Other lives asked humankind:O humans, you who thus roam the world without end,going from one place to another —for what reason do you do so?The people of that time replied:We envy and yearn to fly as the birds do;that is the lullaby (καταβαυκάλησις = singing a lullaby) the Gods softly croon in our dreams.The other lives asked:Have the Gods said something to you?The people answered:The Gods said to us:Embrace the sky (Οὐρανός = Ouranos = Sky, Heaven),touch freedom (ἐλεύθερος = liberty, free),newborn child (παῖς = child).The other lives asked again:How strange you humans are —have you no place that belongs to you?Have you no home?The people wondered in perplexity:Home? What is home?In that age, the boundaries between life and death, between waking and dreaming, were blurred and indistinct.For the people of that time,one generation being born and another generation dying (Θάνατος = Thanatos = Death)was simply one generation waking and another generation falling asleep (Ὕπνος = Hypnos = Sleep).People lived amphibiously between land and sea;people lived amphibiously between waking and dream (ὄνειρος = Oneiros = Dream);people could not tell what difference lay between the two, nor did they seek to.The chance and the necessity met with while waking,the chance and the necessity met with in dream —there was no difference between them.And so it was:generation upon generation blossomed,generation upon generation withered;while waking, some would ponder what home is,and in dream, some too would pursue the question of what home is.Generation after generation, for who knows how long,this question became an unsleeping echo (Ἠχώ = Echo) between the generations.Because of this attention to and curiosity about "home,"people, without being aware of it,began in their dreams to pray to the Gods, asking what "home" is.Devout prayer condensed into the supplications of each person,and these supplications, great and small, embraced one another,gathering into an expedition,from the shallow sea to the deep sea,from faint glimmering light into darkness,in the icy waters of the sea,searching for that legendary abyss (ἄβυσσος = abyss, bottomless depth) whose bottom cannot be seen —where, it was said, the God who truly rules the ocean dwells.When the people awoke,they forgot the prayers to which they had given breath in dream.They had only a faint impression,as though they had asked some question.The stars revolved,and after who knows how long,a new legend circulated in the dreams of the people.That rumor, never heard before, saidthat a beautiful white bull had been born from the farthest end of the deep sea.And then more and more people said they had seen that legendary white bull."Oh! So the white bull is truly real!"And so those who discovered the white bull in the sea followed behind that miraculous creature,and new witnesses joined without cease this ever-swelling procession brimming with curiosity.The people wished to seewhere the beautiful white bull truly wished to go,and whether it had a final destination (τέλος = telos = end, destination, fulfillment).Someone could not help asking the white bull:Beautiful white bull, where are you really going? Are you searching for something?The white bull said:I dreamed of a beautiful seven-colored rainbow (Ἶρις = Iris = Rainbow);in the dream, the rainbow in the vault of heaven was singing to me.The people asked again:So you wish to find the rainbow in the sky —but we cannot fly; when the time comes, may we still follow you?The white bull said:I do not know either.The people who shared the dream with the white bull asked no more, and continued silently to follow.Without clamor or commotion, like an orderly school of fish,they circled the luminous white bull, swimming back and forth in regular rhythm.Light and shadow alternated,and after who knows how long,the white bull said it heard a tremendous sound.Slowly it swam upward,leaving the deep sea,leaving the shallow sea,at last breaking free of the surface,and breathing the air of the land.The multitude of people followed the white bull onto the shore,and they saw, upon the earth beneath a torrential storm, a dreadful and enormous rift (χάσμα = chasma = chasm, rift, gulf),as though struck by a lightning never seen before,the flames it left behind not extinguished even beneath the falling drops of rain.At this moment the white bull seemed to lose all its strength;it knelt upon all four legs, its breathing ever thinner.The people asked it:What is wrong? Are you ill? Should we return to the sea?The white bull answered:Thank you,but I think I shall soon die;my life is ebbing away without cease.Perhaps this is my end (τέλος = telos = end, destination, fulfillment).The people asked:But what of the rainbow?Did you not say you would find the rainbow?We have not yet seen the rainbow.The white bull said:Dear friends,I can still hear the song of the rainbow (ᾠδή = ode = song, ode).Perhaps the final stretch of the road cannot be reached by the body.Could you deliver me to the rainbow's side?This is a pact.The people asked:What must we do?The white bull said:Have your leader of song adorn me;we shall bathe together in pure clean water;then lay gold leaf upon my great horns,and set my strengthless body amid fragrant wood.The people asked:Is that all that is needed?The white bull said:Oh —have your leader of song, amid singing and dancing,take up that flame which does not go out beneath the rain,and set me alight together with the fragrant wood.I shall become formless smoke and fire,and under the witness of the Gods,bearing our hopes with me, I shall behold the rainbow.Please consent to this oath (ὅρκος = oath, sworn pledge) between us,my best friends, faithful companions on the journey of my life.The people asked:But, if that is so, you will die.The white bull said:Dear friends,I have been away from home too long;I too must return home.Please promise methat once I have become smoke,you will share and eat my flesh and blood;this shall become our common memory,a mark passed down through the generations.And the bones I leave behind,and those horns touched with gold leaf —please, by no means take them away;arrange them into a fine and pleasing form,and let them sink beneath that rift into the waters of the sea.My soul shall follow them home (νόστος = nostos = homecoming, return).The people did not understand:Home? What is home?What kind of place is it?The white bull said:Do you not know?The people answered:We do not know.The white bull said:Then please bind the longest rope in the world to my white bones;when the rope falls wholly still,you will know that I have returned home.The people asked again:Then what is home?The white bull answered:Dear friends,returning home and home are different ways of speaking of one and the same thing.So long as you feel the rope fall wholly still,in the moment you know I have returned home,you too will surely understand what home is.The people asked once more:And what of us?When you have died, where should we go?The white bull said:I do not know either.Perhaps, after I have returned home,you might wait and see whether the rainbow appears in the sky,pray to the Gods,and then consider where you wish to go.I am sorrythat I cannot bring you to behold the true rainbow (Ἶρις = Iris = Rainbow),nor invite you back to the place where my dream began.If you should miss me,you may look upon and touch that rope;it is the gravestone and symbol of my rest (σῆμα = sema = sign, mark, tomb, monument),it is the memory in which I and you still take part (μνήμη = mneme = memory, remembrance),and it is the miracle promised by the Gods (θαῦμα = thauma = wonder, marvel).May the Gods protect you.Weeping and laughing,the people, as promised, burned the white bull amid the fragrant wood.The white bull neither suffered nor cried out;only, seeing the people weep for it,it too shed its final tears.A great fire never seen beforedrove away the darkness and the cold.From the still-blazing flames,the people carefully drew forth the white bones the white bull had left behind.The gold leaf upon the horns had not fallen away,but had instead fused into the whole pair of horns,granting them the radiance of pure gold.The other peoples wandering the world,seeing from afar the vast flame,became the final participants in this rite of sacrifice;they were invited to witness (μάρτυς = martyr = witness)how the bones of the white bull sank back through the rift into the deep sea.The people sawthat the longest rope in the world,like a fish drawn out of water,trembled without cease in the dryness,giving forth a sound at every moment,never resting, day after day and night after night.Sun and moon rose and set,life and death turned in their cycle,and no one knows how long again passed —several generations, perhaps? Or perhaps more than ten?Beneath the oath,that rope, already become legend, was still kept watch over by the people.Until one dawn, when most were still asleep in dream,the rope suddenly gave forth no more sound,and fell still.The people, who had long since bid farewell to the amphibious lifeand no longer entered dream within the sea,gazed upon the faint rainbow of the dawn,embracing one another, trembling,and in accordance with the final pact with the white bull,named in remembrance its unseen relic at the far endanchor (ἄγκυρα = anchor).That was the people's final memory of the white bull.

entry.title: Mythos & Kallos · Part 17-18

link.title: Mythos & Kallos · Part 17-18

entry.content:
Mythos & Kallos · Part 17 · Moirai β

B, slightly tipsy, was not entirely clear-headed; B's attention was not upon A's tone of voice, for B's mind had been drawn away and occupied by the music.

The music B heard was somewhat peculiar, giving B a faint yet lingering feeling that would not disperse.

B recalled that a friend had once introduced an instrument called the "Viola d'amore" (viol of love). Like the Sitar, this instrument bears a design of sympathetic resonating strings — the source of the echoing quality within its timbre.

How many years had passed since then? B no longer remembered; the flickering shadows of recollection seemed as though from yesterday.

When B returned to the present, A was telling the story of a scholar who studied funerary customs.

B: My apologies — I was drawn away by the music just now, and seem to have missed much of what you said. Friend, how did you come to speak of funerary customs?

A: Oh, friend — then from where shall I begin the telling anew?

B felt a slight headache, not even knowing where A had reached before B's mind wandered off.

B: To speak honestly, I do not even know how long my mind drifted. To me it seemed but an instant, yet I truly do not know how much time has passed. A person's psychological time and physical time are never synchronized; your rhythm and mine both differ from the world's. Why should this be so?

A: Friend, perhaps we all dwell within "attention" (προσοχή = prosoche = attention, attentiveness)?

B: What you say sounds reasonable. Then why are our paces so full of dislocation?

A: Oh — perhaps we, as spectators seated upon the chariot of "attention" (προσοχή), are all children attending the theatrical festival rites, hearts brimming with expectation yet dazed and uneasy. In truth, I do not understand it either, friend.

B: It is nothing, my friend. Continue your telling; pay me no mind.

A: Very well.

Long, long ago,

there was a scholar of funerary customs, searching through the differences in funeral rites among the various sects of a certain religion.

The scholar noticed that two sects' prayers for the dead, though bearing subtle grammatical differences, were nearly identical in meaning.

This intriguing clue led the researcher to search through ever more archives and documents, until at last the shared origin of these two sects' funeral prayers was traced back to an age of great chaos.

In that age, sects splintered and despised one another.

Different sects would form alliances to oppose sects of greater divergence; and when the common enemy perished, they would sink into a new round of slaughter.

Assassination, plunder, enslavement, the extermination of households, the burning of villages, the massacre of cities — all could occur, even though these sects, in theory, believed in the very same God.

Blood-feuds arose not only between different sects; even within a single sect, a chance friction might kindle the flames of further schism.

Some sects declined from then on, some even perished, leaving in history only a name of interest to none but scholars and antiquarians.

Sunlight spilled into the library, and in the cold weather it brought an inexplicable drowsiness.

"
…Do not fear the void

Sleep, sleep…
"

Do not fear the void? What a strange funeral prayer this is,

thought the one reading.

Thoughts scattered unawares,

the eyelids could no longer be held open,

the breathing grew slower and slower.

The reader fell asleep,

and dreamed a dream.

When did the dream begin?

The drowsy dreamer did not know.

In a world of war and upheaval,

two sects of the same religion formed a temporary alliance,

for they shared a common enemy.

The soldiers of the two sects gathered together,

intending jointly to plunder the monastery of a hostile heretical sect.

They hoped to find valuables within the monastery —

to strike at heresy while easing the army's fiscal burdens and lifting morale.

The soldiers, blessed by the army chaplains,

met no resistance whatsoever upon entering the monastery;

their consecrated weapons found no use.

Most within the monastery had fled;

only a few grey-haired old monks remained.

When the soldiers of both factions scrambled into the inner courtyard,

the old monks were still kneeling upon the ground in prayer.

The soldiers surrounded the monks.

Some of the monks trembled —

from fear,

from anger,

and from sorrow.

"This is holy ground! How dare you enter bearing blades? You are blaspheming against God!"

The old monk who spoke these words was shoved to the ground.

"Silence! Preacher of heresy!"

So said the army chaplain.

At the officer's signal,

the soldiers beat and kicked the old monks,

demanding to know where the monastery's valuables were hidden.

This was, in truth, mere routine procedure —

this monastery had hidden nothing.

Upon receiving word that they had become a target of attack,

the old monks had sent the younger generation fleeing with the scriptures and many books.

With too few hands, only the most important things could be carried away.

"Do not look back, young ones, and do not attempt to return. Our inheritance is entrusted to you. Go now — God be with you."

This was the final command of the old ones who had resolved to remain.

"You cannot take these! These are the offerings of devout believers, sacrifices for the glory of God!" said one old monk.

"Nonsense! All of this is ill-gotten wealth, gathered by bewitching the masses!"

Vessels of gold, vessels of silver, and many other valuables

were swept into sacks under the mutual surveillance of the two sects' soldiers.

When all was finished, these goods would be divided equally;

private concealment was an absolute crime, punished by immediate death.

This was not a wealthy monastery,

but whatever could be scraped together was better than nothing.

After all, the operation had cost no casualties whatsoever —

against a cost of zero, this was infinite gain.

The leading old monk, who had remained silent even under the beating, blood at the corner of the mouth, said in an aged voice:

"Lay these down, children…

You know not what you do…

Children, turn back — there is still time…

God will forgive you…"

The old monk's voice was too faint; even had it been heard, not a single person would have cared.

When the plundering was complete, the chaplains and officers ordered all the monks killed —

the reason given: this was God's purification,

and the sinful souls gone astray required deliverance.

And besides —

what war exists in which no one dies?

A war without death is merely a children's game.

Only, those who gave the order

seemed not quite to dare carry out the executions within the inner courtyard,

and commanded the soldiers to drag the monks to the outer courtyard for the death sentence.

The leading old monk, at the moment of death,

still gripped fast in hand an old, broken piece of wood,

soundlessly reciting:

"
Do not fear the departing far

Do not fear the breath going out

Do not fear the soundlessness

Do not fear the darkness

Do not fear the void (κενόν = kenon = void, emptiness)

Sleep, sleep…
"

At the second "sleep,"

the old monk's life was ended,

and breath was no more.

Though neither sect had suffered any casualties,

the atmosphere remained subtly taut.

The chaplain of one faction

suddenly ordered the monastery set aflame.

The tacit accord of the plundering was broken in that moment,

and the cooperating parties fell into their first disagreement.

"Wait — there is no need to burn this place."

"The grass must be cut and the roots torn out."

"A great fire will draw other heretics here!"

"Let us each simply withdraw with haste."

"Your garrison lies nearer — what of us?"

"I did not expect you to be so weak."

"What did you say? Dare you say it again?"

The soldiers all felt the air drawing ever closer to drawn blades;

some instinctively reached toward their weapons, ready at any moment for battle.

An older officer, seeing matters turn ill, intervened in the quarrel between the two sides' priests.

"Stop, stop, stop! First divide the goods. Once divided, those who wish to burn may burn, and those who do not may withdraw — will that suffice?"

"Then let us divide first."

In the icy cold wind,

both sides divided the spoils,

and no one spoke again of burning the monastery.

The priests of one faction

had the soldiers hastily bury the monks' corpses.

This order to bury the bodies

nearly ignited conflict once more.

In the end, it was the rational reason — "this will prevent plague" — that left the objectors without reply.

For everyone feared plague:

this was not merely a matter of medicine and hygiene,

but a theological terror.

The side stricken by plague

would all too easily be thought cursed, and punished by God.

Both sides, amid suppressed tension and a taut atmosphere,

withdrew in peace without bloodshed,

each returning to their own garrison.

They had cleansed away evil;

they had upheld justice.

The soldiers returned from their extreme emotions to beautiful imaginings of the future:

a small fortune had been made,

wives and children would be pleased —

truly a thing worthy of joy.

Fate and time flowed onward.

Of the generation that plundered the monastery,

some grew old, some died in battle — each life met its own ending.

Under the joint blows of the two sects,

their common enemy was forced to depart the region entirely.

During this time,

sects great and small rose and perished.

Sometimes people heard that an entire town had been massacred;

sometimes people heard that a dreadful plague was spreading in distant lands.
